# Maximum likelihood estimation

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## The likelihood function {.smaller}

Instead of measuring the distance between the curve and the data, we specify a [probability model for the observations]{style="color: tomato;"} and ask how probable the observed counts are under the model with parameters [$\theta$]{style="color: steelblue;"}. This probability, viewed as a function of [$\theta$]{style="color: steelblue;"}, is the [likelihood]{style="color: tomato;"}

::: {style="color: steelblue;"}
$$L(\theta) = \prod_{i=1}^{n} f(y_i \mid \theta)$$
:::

where [$f(y_i \mid \theta)$]{style="color: steelblue;"} is the probability (or density) of observation [$y_i$]{style="color: steelblue;"}, and the product follows from assuming the observations are [conditionally independent]{style="color: tomato;"} given the model. The [maximum likelihood estimate (MLE)]{style="color: tomato;"} is the [$\theta$]{style="color: steelblue;"} that maximises [$L(\theta)$]{style="color: steelblue;"}

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### The log-likelihood

A product of fourteen small probabilities underflows numerically. Taking logarithms turns the product into a sum, the [log-likelihood]{style="color: tomato;"} [$\ell(\theta)$]{style="color: steelblue;"}, which has the same maximiser

::: {style="color: steelblue;"}
$$\hat{\theta} = \arg\max_{\theta} \ell(\theta) = \arg\max_{\theta} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \log f(y_i \mid \theta)$$
:::

Optimisation software minimises by convention, so in practice we minimise the [*negative* log-likelihood]{style="color: tomato;"}

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Advantages of maximum likelihood {.smaller}

- [A principled statistical framework]{style="color: tomato;"}: the likelihood follows from an explicit probability model for the data, so every assumption is stated
- [Uncertainty quantification]{style="color: tomato;"}: the curvature of the log-likelihood at its maximum gives [standard errors]{style="color: tomato;"}, and the [profile likelihood]{style="color: tomato;"} gives confidence intervals
- [Model comparison]{style="color: tomato;"}: models fitted to the same data can be compared through their maximised likelihoods, penalised for complexity by [AIC]{style="color: tomato;"} or [BIC]{style="color: tomato;"}
- [Flexible observation models]{style="color: tomato;"}: Poisson, negative binomial, normal, or whatever matches how the data arise
- [Asymptotic optimality]{style="color: tomato;"}: with enough data the MLE is [consistent, asymptotically normal and efficient]{style="color: tomato;"}

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Choosing an observation model {.smaller}

The data are counts, so the natural choices are

- [Poisson:]{style="color: tomato;"} [$Y_i \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda_i)$]{style="color: steelblue;"}, a single parameter, with variance equal to the mean ([equidispersion]{style="color: tomato;"})
- [Negative binomial:]{style="color: tomato;"} [$Y_i \sim \text{NB}(\mu_i, \phi)$]{style="color: steelblue;"}, with a dispersion parameter [$\phi$]{style="color: steelblue;"} that allows the variance to exceed the mean ([overdispersion]{style="color: tomato;"})

For continuous measurements the usual choices are the normal, [$Y_i \sim N(\mu_i, \sigma^2)$]{style="color: steelblue;"}, or the log-normal, [$\log Y_i \sim N(\log \mu_i, \sigma^2)$]{style="color: steelblue;"}

We start with Poisson, and come back to the negative binomial at the end

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Comparison with least squares

```{.default include="results/04_mle_vs_ls.txt" code-line-numbers="false"}
```

- The two fits are close but not identical: under the Poisson model the variance scales with the mean, so the small counts at the start and end of the outbreak [carry more weight]{style="color: tomato;"} than under the constant variance implied by least squares
- Only the MLE comes with a [confidence interval]{style="color: tomato;"}

## Strengths of maximum likelihood {.smaller}

- A [principled probabilistic framework]{style="color: tomato;"}, with standard errors and confidence intervals as part of the estimate
- [Formal model comparison]{style="color: tomato;"} through likelihood ratios, AIC and BIC, as we have just used it
- [Observation models that match the data]{style="color: tomato;"}: Poisson counts, overdispersed counts, or continuous measurements
- [Asymptotic optimality]{style="color: tomato;"}: with enough data the estimates are as precise as any unbiased estimator can be

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Assumptions and limitations of maximum likelihood {.smaller}

- An explicit [observation model]{style="color: tomato;"} must be specified, and can be [misspecified]{style="color: tomato;"}
- Numerical optimisation requires sensible starting values and can converge to a [local maximum]{style="color: tomato;"}; we started from the least squares fit for exactly that reason
- Standard errors and Wald intervals rest on [asymptotic (large-sample) arguments]{style="color: tomato;"} that fourteen observations may not satisfy; the profile likelihood is more reliable
- [Parameter identifiability]{style="color: tomato;"} is not resolved by the method: the profiles were narrow here only because these data are unusually clean

------------------------------------------------------------------------
